title: Out in haste (Exodus 12:29–42)
hook: no time for the bread to rise; they leave that night

segments.voice: Yesterday, Passover: a lamb, blood on the doorposts, a meal eaten with shoes on. Your line was remember this night. Which family story did you pass on? Day three hundred eighty-seven.

A hurried leaving has a look to it. The phone charger still in the wall. The coffee warm on the counter. The half-packed bag. You take what's in your hands and you go. At midnight in Egypt, the last plague falls. In the King James Bible: "there was a great cry in Egypt; for there was not a house where there was not one dead." Pharaoh's own son among them. And in the middle of the night, the king who said no again and again sends for Moses and Aaron.
screen: `WHAT GETS LEFT BEHIND.` → `MIDNIGHT IN EGYPT.` → `A GREAT CRY.`

segments.voice: Pharaoh says: "Rise up, and get you forth from among my people." Go. Take your flocks. Take everything. And then, from Pharaoh himself: and bless me also. The Egyptians push them out, urging them to hurry. There's no time to finish anything. And Exodus records the detail that people still taste every year: "the people took their dough before it was leavened, their kneadingtroughs being bound up in their clothes upon their shoulders." The bread hadn't risen. So they bake it flat on the road, unleavened cakes, because they were thrust out and could not wait. That flat bread, matzah, is what Jews eat at Passover to this day. It's the taste of leaving before you were ready. Two more details are easy to miss. First: "a mixed multitude went up also with them." Not only Israelites. Others went out with them, and the text doesn't say who they were. Second, the text stops and counts: four hundred and thirty years in Egypt, and on the very day they ended, the people went out. Then it says the night itself belongs to God: "It is a night to be much observed unto the LORD." A night God kept watch over, so Israel keeps watch on it every year. Christians carry the bread forward too. Latin-rite Catholics and some Protestant churches use unleavened bread or wafers at communion, recalling the Passover setting of the Last Supper. Orthodox churches use leavened bread, which Orthodox writers explain as a sign of the risen life. Same table, different loaves.
screen: `RISE UP, AND GET YOU FORTH.` · `DOUGH BEFORE IT WAS LEAVENED.` · `A MIXED MULTITUDE WENT TOO.` · `A NIGHT TO BE MUCH OBSERVED.` · then, large: `UNLEAVENED, IN A HURRY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave one thing unfinished without guilt. Settle, and breathe. Think of the list running in your head right now: emails, laundry, the project, the call. Pick one thing on it that doesn't need finishing today. Picture setting it down, like dough that didn't get to rise. Not failing. Just leaving. Notice how much of your weight is unfinished things. If you pray, you can hand that list to God for two minutes. If you don't, simply put it down. The bell holds the time.
Matzah. Hebrew for unleavened bread, made without yeast: the flat cakes Israel baked in haste, with no time for the dough to rise.
Your line: unleavened, in a hurry. Today, when you're rushing, let one imperfect thing go out the door as it is. Day three hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Jews eat matzah through the week of Passover to remember the hurried departure; Latin-rite Catholics and some Protestant churches use unleavened bread or wafers at communion, while Orthodox churches use leavened bread.

trapdoor: what you thought: unleavened bread is a religious rule about yeast.
what it means: it's the taste of leaving before you were ready, carried on people's shoulders out of slavery.

what a scholar hears: Exodus 12:37–38 gives six hundred thousand men on foot plus a mixed multitude; historians debate those numbers, and Jewish and Christian readers have long discussed who the mixed multitude were.

notes: Communion bread: Latin Catholic use of unleavened hosts, Lutheran and Anglican use of wafers in many places, Orthodox use of leavened bread (prosphora). 'Many Protestant churches' is broad; many use ordinary bread. Confirm.
The 600,000 figure (12:37) and its historical debate appear only in the trapdoor.
'A night God kept watch over' paraphrases the Hebrew sense of 12:42 ('a night of watching'). Confirm.
